title: Morphological, Radiographic and Three-Dimensional Scanning Characterization of the Skull and Mandible of the American Crocodile (Crocodylus acutus).
abstract: The American crocodile (Crocodylus acutus) is a widely distributed Neotropical species for which detailed osteological descriptions of the skull and mandible remain scarce. This study provides an integrative characterization of the cranial and mandibular complex using gross anatomy, descriptive cranial morphometry, radiography, and three-dimensional (3D) scanning. Four skulls and mandibles from post mortem specimens were prepared following standard osteological procedures, and descriptive cranial measurements were recorded. Radiographic projection allowed visualization of bone margins, cranial sutures, dental alveoli, fenestrae, and articular regions. Three-dimensional models generated through a structured-light 3D scanning workflow documented external contours, choanal margins, temporal and mandibular fenestrae, alveolar borders, and sutural patterns. In dorsal, ventral, lateral, and caudal views, the examined skulls displayed an elongated rostrum, dorsally positioned orbits and external nares, paired supratemporal and lateral temporal fenestrae, and a single occipital condyle. The mandibles exhibited elongated and firmly fused symphyses, pronounced retroarticular processes, and well-defined internal and external mandibular fenestrae. Dental preservation varied among specimens, but tooth spacing, conical morphology, and rostrocaudal size variation could be documented in the preserved series. These findings provide a specimen-based reference for the cranial and mandibular complex of C. acutus by integrating morphological, morphometric, radiographic, and three-dimensional (3D) scanning evidence. The digital models constitute an additional resource for anatomical teaching, comparative studies, and long-term digital documentation of osteological morphology.

title: Association of Polygenic Risk Score for Suicidal Behavior With Ventral Prefrontal Morphology in Bipolar Disorder.
abstract: Background Bipolar disorder (BD) studies consistently implicate the ventral prefrontal cortex (VPFC) in association with suicidal behaviors. A suicidal behavior polygenic risk score (PRS) can now be computed to test whether elevated genetic risk for suicidal behavior is associated with variation in VPFC gray matter and/or suicidal behavior history. Methods We explored relationships among a PRS previously associated with suicidal behavior, VPFC morphology, and suicidal behavior in 376 individuals of European ancestry (mean age 30y; 57% female): 225 with BD (76 suicide attempters (SAs), 149 non-suicide attempters (NSAs)) and 151 healthy control individuals (HCs). We calculated PRS and performed magnetic resonance imaging to assess VPFC (inferior frontal gyrus (IFG) and orbitofrontal cortex) cortical thickness and surface area. Associations were examined among PRS, diagnosis, suicide attempt history, and brain measures. Results Among individuals with BD, those with higher PRS showed decreased right VPFC surface area, primarily due to IFG reductions (p < 0.01). A significant group (SA, NSA, HC)-by-PRS interaction was observed for right IFG cortical surface area (p < 0.05); NSAs with high vs. low PRS had significantly smaller right IFG surface area. The mean PRS was highest for SAs, then NSAs, and lowest for HCs; however, differences did not reach significance. Conclusions These findings suggest this suicide PRS may reflect genetic mechanisms influencing IFG differences in BD. Given the modest sample size, replication of these preliminary findings in large-scale diverse cohorts is required to determine whether including this PRS and/or the corresponding IFG values could improve multimodal BD suicidal behavior prediction algorithms.

title: Hepatic Steatosis in People With Chronic Hepatitis B in Africa: Prevalence, Correlates, and Clinical Significance.
abstract: To address data gaps around metabolic liver disease in Africa, within the Hepatitis B in Africa Collaborative Network (HEPSANET), we evaluated participants with chronic hepatitis B virus infection (CHB) for steatotic liver disease (SLD) using transient elastography with controlled attenuation parameter (CAP). Using multivariable logistic regression, we identified sociodemographic, anthropometric, and clinical associations with SLD (CAP ≥ 248 dB/m), and evaluated whether SLD severity was independently associated with fibrosis. Short-term impacts of SLD on mortality were also assessed with Cox proportional hazards analysis. We also evaluated the diagnostic performance of B-mode ultrasound for SLD, with CAP as reference. Across 6 countries and 1601 participants (age range, 12-80 years; 39.5% female; 4% with diabetes; 11% unhealthy alcohol use; median body mass index, 24.4), 421 (26.3%) had SLD; 219 (13.7%) had severe steatosis (CAP ≥ 280 dB/m). Older age, male sex, overweight and obesity, and HIV-negative status were associated with SLD. After adjusting for age, sex, HIV status, HBV treatment, and country, severe steatosis, but not mild and moderate forms (i.e., 248-279 dB/m), was associated with a 8.4% (95%, 1.9%-14.9%) increased probability of fibrosis. Over limited follow-up (median 2.69 years) and small number of deaths, SLD was not associated with all-cause or liver-related mortality. B-mode ultrasound had low sensitivity for SLD, overall or when severe, but specificity was 95%. In conclusion, SLD was common in people with CHB in Africa and its severe form was associated with liver fibrosis. These data support screening for metabolic comorbidities as part of HBV care and treatment in Africa.

title: Application of Combined Gastric Tube Tip Manometry and Auscultation for Nasogastric Tube Positioning in Neurocritical Care Patients With Artificial Airways: A Prospective Diagnostic Pilot Study.
abstract: Background Nasogastric tube placement is central to enteral nutrition support in neurocritical care patients. However, tube malposition, particularly accidental placement into the airway, can lead to fatal complications. Aim To assess the accuracy of a combined gastric tube tip manometry and auscultation approach for confirming nasogastric tube placement in neurocritical care patients with artificial airways. Study design This prospective study enrolled patients who underwent nasogastric tube insertion in the neurocritical care unit of a tertiary hospital in China between January 2025 and May 2025. Using chest X-ray as the reference standard, we compared the sensitivity, specificity, positive predictive value (PPV), negative predictive value (NPV), positive likelihood ratio (PLR) and negative likelihood ratio (NLR) for gastric tube tip manometry alone, auscultation alone and their combination. Results In total, 120 patients participated. X-ray confirmed correct nasogastric tube positioning in 119 patients and malposition in 1 patient. For gastric tube tip manometry alone, the sensitivity was 97.48%, with a specificity of 0%, a positive predictive value (PPV) of 99.15% and a negative predictive value (NPV) of 0%. Auscultation alone yielded a sensitivity of 90.76%, a specificity of 100%, a PPV of 100% and an NPV of 8.33%. The combined manometry-plus-auscultation approach had a sensitivity of 88.24%, a specificity of 100%, a PPV of 100% and an NPV of 6.67%. Conclusions The combined gastric tube tip manometry and auscultation method might serve as an adjunctive bedside strategy for confirming nasogastric tube placement in neurocritical care patients with artificial airways. However, only one malpositioned tube was observed in this study; the specificity and NPV should be interpreted with caution. Relevance to clinical practice When gastric aspirate cannot be obtained or immediate chest radiography is impractical, combined gastric tube tip manometry and auscultation provide a feasible, radiation-free bedside pathway for confirming nasogastric tube position; equivocal or negative bedside findings should still be verified radiographically before feeding. Trial registration The study was registered with the Chinese Clinical Trial Registry (ChiCTR2300078001).

In total, 120 patients participated. X-ray confirmed correct nasogastric tube positioning in 119 patients and malposition in 1 patient. For gastric tube tip manometry alone, the sensitivity was 97.48%, with a specificity of 0%, a positive predictive value (PPV) of 99.15% and a negative predictive value (NPV) of 0%. title: Concurrent Long Thoracic and Lateral Cutaneous Intercostal Nerve Entrapment After Chest Tube Thoracostomy Causing Scapular Winging and Chest Wall Pain: Diagnosis With Ultrasound and Treatment With Hydrodissection.
abstract: Background Chest tube thoracostomy may cause iatrogenic nerve injury, resulting in persistent pain and functional impairment. Long thoracic nerve (LTN) palsy after chest tube placement has been described, but concurrent involvement of the LTN and the lateral cutaneous branch of an intercostal nerve (LCIN) appears to be rarely reported. We describe a patient with persistent post-thoracostomy chest wall pain and scapular winging in whom musculoskeletal ultrasonography identified entrapment of both nerves. Case presentation A 43-year-old man presented with severe left shoulder and chest wall pain 6 months after chest tube placement for traumatic hemopneumothorax. Examination demonstrated focal tenderness, dysesthesia, and mechanical allodynia at the chest tube scar, along with medial/inferior scapular winging during serratus anterior provocative testing. Shoulder range of motion was full on examination; however, forward flexion beyond 15° markedly aggravated pain, resulting in pain-related reluctance to move the shoulder. Manual muscle testing was 4+/5 before treatment because pain limited force generation. Musculoskeletal ultrasound demonstrated focal abnormality of the LTN where it pierced the axillary fascia over the sixth rib, with loss of fascicular definition and reduced glide, and tethering/thickening of the LCIN within scar tissue at the prior tube insertion site. Symptom reproduction with sonopalpation supported the clinical relevance of both findings. Intervention and results Ultrasound-guided hydrodissection using 5% dextrose in water was performed around both nerves. A total of approximately 40 mL of 5% dextrose in water was used, with 20 mL administered per nerve. Immediately after the first procedure, pain improved from NRS 9/10 to 2/10, with marked reduction in pain during shoulder movement, including forward flexion. The patient subsequently underwent 5 treatment sessions at 2-week intervals over 10 weeks. During follow-up, manual muscle testing improved to 5/5 without pain, scapular winging was no longer evident on provocative testing, and the Shoulder Pain and Disability Index improved from pain/disability scores of 25/15 to 6/4. At the sixth follow-up visit, pain and function were satisfactory, and the patient elected continued monitoring without further intervention. At 1-year follow-up, treatment efficacy remained sustained without recurrence. Conclusion In patients with persistent shoulder or chest wall pain after chest tube thoracostomy, iatrogenic peripheral nerve entrapment should be considered. This case highlights the value of a focused neuromuscular examination and musculoskeletal ultrasound for identifying concurrent motor and sensory nerve involvement and suggests that ultrasound-guided hydrodissection may be a useful minimally invasive treatment. Because electrodiagnostic studies were not performed, the findings are most consistent with entrapment/neurapraxia with dynamic tethering rather than electrodiagnostically proven axonal palsy.

title: Meibomian Gland Epithelioma Mimicking Eyelid Squamous Cell Carcinoma in a Hereford-Cross Steer.
abstract: Objective To describe the clinical presentation and histopathology of a meibomian gland epithelioma that clinically resembled squamous cell carcinoma in a steer. Animal studied A 15 year-old Hereford-Lowline cross steer presented for evaluation of an approximately 2 × 4 cm ulcerated, pedunculated eyelid mass arising from the right inferior eyelid margin. Procedures Excision of the mass followed by adjunctive cryotherapy was performed. The mass was submitted for histopathologic analysis. Results Histopathologic evaluation revealed the mass to be consistent with a meibomian gland epithelioma, a neoplastic proliferation of the basal/reserve cells of the meibomian gland. The steer recovered routinely from the procedure with no evidence of regrowth of the mass at 13 months post-operatively. Conclusion Meibomian gland epitheliomas are one of the most common eyelid tumors of dogs; however, this is the first known report of a histologically confirmed meibomian gland epithelioma in cattle. Clinically, the mass resembled the appearance of squamous cell carcinoma, a common eyelid tumor in Hereford cattle. The clinical misclassification of a benign eyelid mass as squamous cell carcinoma could lead to unnecessary aggressive management such as enucleation, exenteration, or culling. This case confirms the importance of histopathologic analysis of excised tissues to reach an accurate diagnosis and appropriate treatment and follow-up plans.

title: Idiopathic Granulomatous Inflammation of the Periocular Structures in Four Dogs: Clinical, Histopathological, and Imaging Findings and Therapeutic Outcome.
abstract: Purpose To describe cases of canine idiopathic periocular granulomatous inflammation. Material and methods Clinical records were reviewed. Animal studied At the time of presentation, the four patients (German Shepherd dog, mixed breed, Magyar Vizsla, Hovawart) were 1.5-5 (mean 3.75) years old. All dogs were female; two were spayed. Lesions were unilateral in 3/4 cases. Dogs presented with ulcerated (1) or non-ulcerated (3) mass lesions affecting the periocular skin (3/4), medial canthal area (2/4), or third eyelid (1/4). Results Incisional biopsies revealed pyogranulomatous inflammation in three and granulomatous inflammation in one case. There was no evidence of microbial infection in the specimens. Patients received anti-inflammatory or immunosuppressive dosages of systemic corticosteroids. Three dogs also received systemic cyclosporin (5 mg/kg, sid), and one dog received topical cyclosporin (0.1%, bid). One dog underwent surgical debulking of a circumscribed mass within the left lower eyelid prior to immunosuppressive therapy and developed an additional swelling on the left upper eyelid. Remission of clinical signs was achieved in all patients. Dogs were treated for 5 to 11 months (mean 8.7). No recurrence was reported in 4/4 patients during a mean follow-up period of 17.3 months. In 3/4patients, there was no recurrence within an average of 11 months after discontinuation of therapy. One dog was lost to follow-up. Conclusion Idiopathic granulomatous inflammation is a differential diagnosis for periocular mass lesions. Its diagnosis is based on histopathology and the exclusion of other causes of granulomatous inflammation.

One dog underwent surgical debulking of a circumscribed mass within the left lower eyelid prior to immunosuppressive therapy and developed an additional swelling on the left upper eyelid. Remission of clinical signs was achieved in all patients. Dogs were treated for 5 to 11 months (mean 8.7). No recurrence was reported in 4/4 patients during a mean follow-up period of 17.3 months. In 3/4patients, there was no recurrence within an average of 11 months after discontinuation of therapy. One dog was lost to follow-up.

Conclusion

Idiopathic granulomatous inflammation is a differential diagnosis for periocular mass lesions. Its diagnosis is based on histopathology and the exclusion of other causes of granulomatous inflammation.

title: Bilateral Keratouveitis and Secondary Glaucoma in a Young Dog With Immune-Mediated Polyarthritis and Systemic Inflammatory Response Syndrome.
abstract: A 7-month-old intact female mixed-breed dog presented emergently for inability to walk, lethargy, and vomiting. The patient was diagnosed with immune-mediated polyarthritis (IMPA) and secondary systemic inflammatory response syndrome (SIRS). Bilateral keratouveitis and secondary glaucoma developed within 24 h of presentation. Thorough diagnostic testing failed to identify an underlying etiology. Despite aggressive medical management, the patient developed rapid vision loss. Due to poor visual prognosis and anticipated need for long-term medical management, both eyes were enucleated. Histopathological evaluation of both globes revealed severe corneal endothelial injury most consistent with endotheliitis with associated uveitis and endophthalmitis. Testing of ocular tissue with PCR and immunohistochemistry for canine adenovirus was negative, and comprehensive infectious disease screening, joint cultures, and ocular histopathology identified no other causative agents. Following enucleation, the dog systemically improved with anti-inflammatory and antimicrobial medical management. This report highlights a unique and severe case of bilateral keratouveitis with glaucoma following a systemic inflammatory event.

title: Computed Tomographic Findings of Hepatic Rupture Associated With Amyloidosis in a Young Siamese Cat.
abstract: A 3-year-old neutered male Siamese cat with chronic anorexia showed anemia and elevated liver enzyme levels. Ultrasonography disclosed multiple diffusely heterogeneous hepatic lesions and peritoneal effusion, which was identified as hemoabdomen upon fluid analysis. Computed tomography showed finger-like hypoattenuation extending from the left hepatic margin with focal margin loss in the delayed phase, suggesting hepatic rupture. Infiltrative hepatic diseases were considered, and amyloidosis was the top differential diagnosis given the patient's young age, breed predisposition, and suspected hepatic rupture. Blood oozing was confirmed via laparotomy, and Congo red staining established hepatic amyloidosis, though amyloid typing was not pursued.

title: Radiographic Comparison of Pulmonary Lobar Vasculature Dimensions in Medically Managed and Drug-Naive Dogs With Left Heart Failure Secondary to Myxomatous Mitral Valve Disease.
abstract: Myxomatous mitral valve disease (MMVD) is the most common acquired cause of left heart failure (LHF) in dogs, and radiographic identification of pulmonary venous enlargement is traditionally used to support the diagnosis of LHF. However, the absence of venous enlargement has been anecdotally observed after initiation of therapy. Therefore, we aimed to compare radiographic pulmonary vessel size in LHF patients with ongoing medical management ± receiving acute rescue therapy. Dogs with echocardiographically confirmed MMVD and radiographic cardiogenic pulmonary edema were retrospectively selected. Pulmonary lobar artery and vein widths were measured using standardized rib-to-vessel ratios: cranial vessels at the intersection with the fourth rib on lateral projections and caudal vessels at the ninth rib on ventrodorsal/dorsoventral projections. Pulmonary vein-to-artery (PV/PA) and vessel-to-rib ratios were calculated, with enlargement defined as >1.2 and small vessel size as <0.8, and treatment groups were compared using Welch-corrected t-tests. 200 radiographic studies from 163 dogs were reviewed. In all dogs, the veins measured larger than the arteries in all lung lobes. Chronically untreated dogs who received furosemide immediately before radiographs had no venous enlargement. All other groups had vascular asymmetry or venous enlargement in at least two lung lobes. All control dogs with reoccurrence of LHF had absence of venous enlargement after initiation of therapy. Pulmonary venous enlargement was most pronounced in the right caudal lung lobe. These findings indicate that dogs chronically managed for MMVD may decompensate into LHF without radiographic pulmonary venous enlargement and that furosemide administration prior to imaging can normalize vessel size.

title: Computed Tomographic Findings of Ischemic Necrosis of the Accessory Carpal Bone in a Dog.
abstract: A 1-year-and-9-month-old Golden Retriever presented with a 9-month history of right thoracic limb lameness. Radiographs revealed a monostotic, expansile lesion of the right accessory carpal bone (ACB). A computed tomography (CT) confirmed the aggressive nature of the lesion, demonstrating multifocal moth-eaten osteolysis, sclerosis, periosteal reaction, and flexor carpi ulnaris tendinopathy. Differential diagnoses included the ischemic necrosis of the ACB, osteomyelitis, and primary bone neoplasia. Histopathology confirmed osteonecrosis. This case highlights the value of CT in evaluating aggressive carpal lesions and identifies ischemic necrosis as an important differential diagnosis. This case represents the first CT description of this disease in dogs.

title: Agreement of Multimodal Large Language Models and Novice Readers With Expert-Based Radiographic Scoring of Presumptive Septic Carpal Arthritis in Calves.
abstract: Septic arthritis is an important cause of morbidity in calves, and radiographic interpretation may vary between observers, especially when structured scoring systems are used by less experienced readers. This single-center retrospective reader study evaluated whether general-purpose multimodal large language models (LLMs) could support rubric-based radiographic scoring of presumptive septic carpal arthritis in calves. Fifty calves aged 0-3 months with clinical findings consistent with presumptive septic carpal arthritis were included, and one carpal radiograph per case was assessed. Two novice veterinary surgeons and three multimodal LLMs, ChatGPT-5, Gemini-2.5 Pro, and Claude Sonnet-4, independently scored each case using a Constant-based ordinal radiographic scoring framework. Expert consensus served as the operational reference standard. Agreement with the reference was assessed using exact agreement, agreement within one score category, and quadratic weighted kappa. Novice 1 showed the highest concordance, with a mean exact agreement of 55.6%, mean ±1 agreement of 89.8%, and substantial agreement (mean κ w = 0.68; 95% CI, 0.56-0.80). ChatGPT-5 was the best-performing model, achieving moderate agreement (mean exact agreement, 53.0%; mean ±1 agreement, 82.6%; mean κ w = 0.58; 95% CI, 0.41-0.72). Claude Sonnet-4 and Gemini-2.5 Pro showed slight agreement overall. The best-performing novice reader remained more reliable than the evaluated models, although ChatGPT-5 performed comparably to, or better than, one novice evaluator in selected parameters. Selected LLMs may have limited adjunctive value for structured review or training, but not as replacements for human interpretation.

title: Evaluation of Intracranial Lesions Using Deep Learning-Based Reconstruction in Canine Brain MRI: Comparison With Conventional Reconstruction on T2-Weighted and FLAIR Sequences.
abstract: Obtaining high-resolution brain MRI in small animals is challenging due to the inherent trade-off between image quality and acquisition time. Deep learning-based reconstruction (DLR) has emerged as a solution to improve image quality without prolonging scan time; however, its clinical utility and potential risks, such as pseudolesions, remain insufficiently evaluated in veterinary patients. This study aimed to evaluate the impact of DLR on lesion assessment and image quality in canine brain MRI and to investigate potential limitations associated with its application. This retrospective study compared DLR with conventional reconstruction in 25 canine brain MRI examinations diagnosed with intracranial diseases. Transverse T2-weighted and fluid-attenuated inversion recovery sequences were reconstructed using both conventional and DLR methods. Quantitative analysis included signal-to-noise ratio (SNR), contrast-to-noise ratio (CNR), and lesion edge sharpness. Two blinded radiologists assessed image quality, lesion conspicuity, artifacts, pseudolesions, and lesion masking. DLR images exhibited significantly higher SNR, CNR, and lesion edge sharpness than conventional images in both sequences (p < 0.05). DLR images also yielded significantly higher qualitative scores for image quality and lesion conspicuity (p < 0.05). Truncation artifact was significantly reduced, whereas motion and pulsation artifacts showed no improvement. No instances of pseudolesions or lesion masking were noted. DLR significantly improves image quality and lesion conspicuity in canine brain MRI and reduces truncation artifacts; however, it does not mitigate motion or pulsation interference. Collectively, these findings suggest that DLR has potential value for improving image quality and lesion visibility in canine brain MRI, whereas further studies are needed to determine its impact on diagnostic performance.

title: Radiologic Evaluation of the Nasopharynx: A Comprehensive Review.
abstract: The nasopharynx is a critical component of the upper aerodigestive tract and has essential roles in respiration, auditory tube function, and speech resonance. Accurate imaging evaluation of this region allows assessment of deeper structures that cannot be evaluated by clinical examination alone. A thorough understanding of nasopharyngeal anatomy, embryology, and the spectrum of benign and malignant diseases is vital for accurate diagnosis. Key imaging features may be identified across CT and MRI modalities. Although CT effectively delineates local bone and soft-tissue structures, MRI provides superior soft-tissue characterization and allows better assessment of soft-tissue lesions and tumor extension. Disorders affecting the nasopharynx and surrounding structures include eustachian tube dysfunction, cystic lesions, anatomic variations of the clivus, and inflammatory and infectious conditions, as well as neoplasms such as nasopharyngeal carcinoma and lymphoma. Recognizing imaging pearls and pitfalls is useful for accurate diagnosis and to distinguish benign from malignant entities. Optimal patient management-including accurate radiologic diagnosis, early detection of malignancies, differential diagnosis, assessment of disease extent, and posttreatment surveillance-can be achieved through comprehensive radiologic evaluation. © RSNA, 2026 Supplemental material is available for this article.

title: Comprehensive Imaging Review of the Ureter.
abstract: The ureter is an important conduit between the kidney and the bladder and is frequently imaged to rule out cancer in the upper genitourinary tract. However, while malignancy can occur, a spectrum of other pathologic ureteral findings can exist, and these can be divided into congenital, intrinsic, and extrinsic abnormalities that range from postoperative and neoplastic conditions to inflammatory disease. This article provides a comprehensive overview of the ureter, including the ureteral anatomy, ureteral imaging strategies, and various ureteral conditions and their associated imaging features. It is important to identify congenital genitourinary variants, as these are frequently linked to further imaging recommendations, such as nuclear medicine renography and fluoroscopic voiding cystourethrography. Intrinsic abnormalities can be iatrogenic, infectious, inflammatory, or neoplastic. Intrinsic ureteral strictures are most commonly iatrogenic, usually resulting from prior surgery or radiation therapy. Ureteral infections include tuberculosis, schistosomiasis, and Escherichia coli infection, which have varying imaging manifestations. Inflammatory conditions include ureteritis cystica and pseudodiverticulosis. Ureteral masses are rarely benign and are most commonly urothelial carcinomas. Processes in the abdomen and pelvis, including mass effect from pregnancy, ureteral compression from advanced pelvic floor prolapse, and rarely, ureteral obstruction from vaginal devices, also can affect the ureter. The ureter can be injured during pelvic surgery or trauma. It also may be involved by deep pelvic endometriosis, mass effect from extrinsic lesions, or reactive change from inflammatory processes. Radiologists need to have a clear understanding of the patient's history and the range of possible ureteral conditions to establish the optimal differential diagnosis.

This article provides a comprehensive overview of the ureter, including the ureteral anatomy, ureteral imaging strategies, and various ureteral conditions and their associated imaging features. It is important to identify congenital genitourinary variants, as these are frequently linked to further imaging recommendations, such as nuclear medicine renography and fluoroscopic voiding cystourethrography. Intrinsic abnormalities can be iatrogenic, infectious, inflammatory, or neoplastic. Intrinsic ureteral strictures are most commonly iatrogenic, usually resulting from prior surgery or radiation therapy. Ureteral infections include tuberculosis, schistosomiasis, and Escherichia coli infection, which have varying imaging manifestations. Inflammatory conditions include ureteritis cystica and pseudodiverticulosis. Ureteral masses are rarely benign and are most commonly urothelial carcinomas. Processes in the abdomen and pelvis, including mass effect from pregnancy, ureteral compression from advanced pelvic floor prolapse, and rarely, ureteral obstruction from vaginal devices, also can affect the ureter. The ureter can be injured during pelvic surgery or trauma. It also may be involved by deep pelvic endometriosis, mass effect from extrinsic lesions, or reactive change from inflammatory processes. Radiologists need to have a clear understanding of the patient's history and the range of possible ureteral conditions to establish the optimal differential diagnosis.

title: MR Neurography of Fine-Caliber Nerves: Technical Considerations and Practical Applications.
abstract: MR neurography (MRN) is a powerful tool for evaluating peripheral nerve disorders, traditionally focused on larger nerves like the sciatic nerve, lumbosacral plexus, and brachial plexus. With advances in hardware and software and improved vascular signal suppression, MRN enables reliable assessment of fine-caliber nerves-defined as those with a diameter of up to 6 mm. The small size, variable anatomy, and proximity to vessels and soft-tissue lesions make imaging of such nerves particularly challenging at routine MRI. The authors focus on MRN of fine-caliber nerves throughout the body, offering technical guidance and case-based examples for practical applications. The MRN protocol should include high-resolution two-dimensional and three-dimensional (3D) isotropic acquisitions, with a tailored field of view and appropriate coil selection. Vascular signal suppression is critical and can be achieved using noncontrast or contrast-enhanced techniques, such as postcontrast short τ inversion-recovery (STIR) or steady-state sequences. Sequence optimization, considering parameters like echo time, fat suppression, spatial resolution, and echo train length, is essential to improve nerve conspicuity. A structured approach to imaging and reporting the most clinically relevant fine-caliber peripheral nerves is presented, highlighting protocol suggestions, key anatomic landmarks, and common lesion sites. By applying dedicated imaging protocols with advanced 3D techniques, radiologists can enhance detection of fine-caliber nerve lesions and provide more confident imaging guidance for clinical decision making and treatment planning. © RSNA, 2026 Supplemental material is available for this article.

title: Multimodal Transformer Integrating CT and Pathology for Postoperative Risk Stratification in Stage I Non-Small Cell Lung Cancer.
abstract: Purpose To develop and evaluate an interpretable, multimodal deep learning model to improve postoperative risk stratification and predict adjuvant therapy benefit in stage I non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC). Materials and Methods In this multicenter retrospective study of patients with stage I NSCLC, a multimodal model called the Deep Learning-Radiomic-Text Transformer (DLRTransformer) was developed by integrating multiview 2.5-dimensional deep learning features from CT scans, radiomics, clinical variables, and prognostic embeddings extracted from pathology reports using a large language model. A central transformer architecture fuses these features to predict disease-free survival. Model performance was evaluated on independent external datasets and compared with guideline-based risk stratification. Associations between model-derived risk scores and tumor microenvironment features were analyzed to assess biologic interpretability. Results A total of 1073 patients (mean age ± SD, 60.8 years ± 9.8; 550 male) were enrolled from five centers. On external datasets, DLRTransformer demonstrated robust prognostic performance (concordance index, 0.77-0.78), outperforming the guideline-based risk stratification (concordance index, 0.60-0.65). Risk scores were associated with tumor microenvironment phenotypes, including increased neoplastic cellularity and reduced tertiary lymphoid structures. A treatment-by-risk interaction was observed (interaction hazard ratio [HR], 0.14; 95% CI: 0.06, 0.32; P < .01). In propensity score-matched subcohorts, adjuvant therapy improved disease-free survival in high-risk patients (HR, 0.30; 95% CI: 0.11, 0.84; P = .02) but not in low-risk patients (HR, 1.70; 95% CI: 0.97, 2.99; P = .06). Conclusion The DLRTransformer improved postoperative risk stratification compared with guideline-based risk stratification and identified patients with stage I NSCLC who benefited from adjuvant therapy.

title: Management, Upgrade Rates, and Radiologic Surveillance of Screen-Detected High-Risk Breast Lesions.
abstract: Purpose To evaluate the prevalence, upgrade rate, and radiologic surveillance management of high-risk lesions (HRLs) detected at screening mammography in a Dutch breast cancer screening population. Materials and Methods This retrospective analysis of a prospectively maintained database included patients recalled from the Dutch breast cancer screening program between January 2009 and July 2019. Incidence rates, diagnostic work-up, radiologic surveillance, and upgrades to (pre)malignancy after surgical excision and during radiologic surveillance were evaluated. Results Among 17 809 recalled patients, 514 patients with a mean age of 58 years ± 8.1 (SD) were diagnosed with an HRL. The incidence rate of HRLs was 0.83 per 1000 screens and 2.89 per 100 recalls. The majority of HRLs consisted of papillary lesions (34.4% [177 of 514]) and atypical ductal hyperplasia (ADH) (31.1% [160 of 514]). Surgical excision was performed in 233 cases (45.3%), resulting in 58 HRLs (24.9%) being upgraded to (pre)malignancy. Invasive tumors were mainly found in papillary lesions with atypia and ADH. Of patients diagnosed with an HRL, 324 (63.0%) had an indication for radiologic surveillance. Of these, 257 (79.3%) underwent surveillance, with 109 (42.4%) completing the recommended 5-year surveillance trajectory. During surveillance, 26 patients (10.1%) developed a (pre)malignancy. Invasive tumors were more frequently identified among HRLs upgraded during surveillance than among HRLs upgraded after surgical excision (17 of 26 [65%] vs 16 of 58 [28%]; P = .001). HRLs upgraded to invasive cancer were more likely to be triple-negative compared with screen-detected cancers (9.1% [3 of 33] vs 6.6% [215 of 3277]; P < .001). Conclusion Overall, 16.3% (84 of 514) of screen-detected HRLs were associated with a diagnosis of (pre)malignancy after surgical excision or during radiologic surveillance. Completion of the recommended 5-year surveillance trajectory was achieved in fewer than half of patients undergoing surveillance. Keywords: Breast Mammography, MR-Imaging, Ultrasound, Biopsy/Needle Aspiration, Screening Supplemental material is available for this article. © RSNA, 2026.

title: Risk-adapted MRI Protocols for the Detection of Clinically Significant Prostate Cancer.
abstract: Purpose To compare the diagnostic performance and clinical utility of three MRI protocols for detecting clinically significant prostate cancer (csPCa) according to prebiopsy risk. Materials and Methods This retrospective study included 390 male patients who underwent prostate multiparametric MRI (mpMRI) between January 2019 and April 2024 for suspected csPCa, followed by biopsy. Patients were stratified by Rotterdam Prostate Cancer Risk Calculator score into low-risk (<4%), intermediate-risk (4%-9%), and high-risk (≥10%) groups. Three datasets were generated from each examination: mpMRI (T2-weighted imaging, diffusion-weighted imaging [DWI], and dynamic contrast-enhanced imaging), unenhanced MRI (multiplanar T2-weighted imaging and DWI), and short MRI (axial T2-weighted imaging and DWI). Overall, 1170 datasets were randomly assigned to 10 expert radiologists (117 examinations each). Diagnostic performance for grade group 2 or greater cancer and clinical utility metrics were compared across risk groups. Results Among the 390 patients (median age, 66 years [IQR, 61-71 years]), csPCa prevalence was 34.4% (134 of 390). In low-risk patients, short MRI demonstrated the highest sensitivity (95% [21 of 22]), with no significant differences among protocols (all P ≥ .21) and greatest potential for safe biopsy avoidance (84 biopsies avoided per missed csPCa). In intermediate-risk patients, mpMRI showed higher sensitivity (83% vs 72% for unenhanced MRI and 62% for short MRI; P = .012 for mpMRI vs short MRI) and higher biopsy efficiency (1.11 vs 0.85 for mpMRI vs unenhanced MRI). In high-risk patients, protocol-related differences were minimal (all P ≥ .12). Conclusion mpMRI was associated with improved sensitivity and biopsy efficiency in intermediate-risk patients, whereas protocol differences were limited in low- and high-risk groups; these findings support risk-adapted selection of MRI protocols. Keywords: MR-Dynamic Contrast-enhanced, MR Imaging, Urinary, Prostate, Neoplasms-Primary, Efficacy Studies, Prostatic Neoplasms, MRI, Contrast Medium, Biopsy, Risk Assessment Supplemental material is available for this article. © RSNA, 2026.

title: Causes of False-Negative Screening Digital Breast Tomosynthesis Examinations: A Multireader Study.
abstract: Purpose To classify the causes and pathologic characteristics of false-negative screening digital breast tomosynthesis examinations. Materials and Methods All false-negative screening examinations at a single center from March 1, 2019, through December 31, 2023, were collected. Seven fellowship-trained breast radiologists independently reviewed the false-negative screening and diagnostic mammograms preceding biopsy. For each mammogram, radiologists recorded the cancer as visible or not visible. Cancers were classified as mammographically occult (not visible on mammogram), missed (visible on screening mammogram), or true interval cancers (visible on diagnostic mammogram only). Between-classification comparisons were performed with the Pearson χ 2 test or analysis of variance. Results A total of 117 female patients (median age, 60 years [IQR, 49-70 years]) with false-negative screening mammograms were included. Most cancers manifested symptomatically (88 of 117, 75.2%) a median of 237 days (IQR, 187-301 days) after screening mammography. Among cancers, 47.9% (56 of 117), 26.5% (31 of 117), and 25.6% (30 of 117) were missed, mammographically occult, and true interval cancers, respectively. True interval cancers were more often estrogen receptor- (50.0% [15 of 30] vs 16.1% [five of 31] vs 21.8% [12 of 55]) and progesterone receptor-negative (66.7% [20 of 30] vs 22.6% [seven of 31] vs 35.7% [20 of 56]) than mammographically occult and missed cancers. Mammographically occult cancers were more often stage T0 (32.3% [10 of 31] vs 7.1% [four of 56] vs 10.0% [three of 30]) and detected at MRI (48.4% [15 of 31] vs 3.6% [two of 56] vs 10.0% [three of 30]) and developed in younger female patients (51 vs 62 vs 59 years of age, all P < .05) than missed and true interval cancers. Conclusion Half of false-negative screening mammograms were missed, one-quarter were true interval, and one-quarter were mammographically occult cancer, with differences in pathologic characteristics. title: Robotic Flexible Ureteroscopy: A Step-by-Step Guide to the ILY® Platform.
abstract: Introduction Robotic flexible ureteroscopy (rfURS) is emerging as an alternative to manual flexible ureteroscopy for the treatment of upper urinary tract stones. Contemporary guidelines and reviews describe its potential ergonomic and radiation-related advantages, as well as comparable surgical outcomes (1-5). Initial clinical and simulation studies with the ILY® platform have demonstrated feasibility, safety, and a short learning curve, although standardized implementation remains limited (6-10). This video presents a step-by-step workflow for the safe and efficient use of the ILY® platform. Materials and methods A 43-year-old woman with a previous right double-J stent placed for obstructive pyelonephritis underwent rfURS for a 13-mm renal pelvic stone (1,497 HU; volume 1,214 mm³). The video demonstrates operating-room setup, robot calibration and sterile draping, robot positioning and fixation, docking to the ureteral access sheath and ureteroscope assembly, console-controlled navigation, laser lithotripsy, systematic renal inspection, and standardized undocking. A flexible suction sheath was used throughout the procedure. Results Draping and docking times were 167 and 645 seconds, respectively. Robotic console time was 115 minutes, including 52 minutes of laser lithotripsy at 8 Hz and 1.2 J. Basket extraction was not required. Undocking was completed in 74 seconds, and total operative time was 130 minutes. No intraoperative complications or troubleshooting events occurred. Postoperative day-1 computed tomography confirmed stone-free status. The patient was discharged at 36 hours postoperatively without complications, as graded by the Clavien-Dindo classification (11). Surgeon satisfaction was rated 8 out of 10. Conclusion rfURS using the ILY® platform was feasible, safe, and effective. A standardized step-by-step workflow may facilitate adoption, improve procedural consistency, and enhance surgeon ergonomics (12). rfURS represents a meaningful step toward autonomous surgery (13).

title: Outcome of Children Treated with Rituximab for Steroid-Resistant Nephrotic Syndrome: Renal Histopathology as a Response Marker.
abstract: Background Steroid-resistant nephrotic syndrome (SRNS) in children remains a major therapeutic challenge. Although calcineurin inhibitors (CNIs) are commonly used as first-line therapy, a substantial proportion of patients fail to achieve remission, and prolonged use may result in nephrotoxicity. Rituximab has emerged as a potential therapeutic option for refractory SRNS; however, treatment responses appear variable, and the influence of underlying renal histopathology remains incompletely understood. Objectives To evaluate the association between renal histopathological findings and clinical response to rituximab in children with calcineurin inhibitor-resistant steroid-resistant nephrotic syndrome (SRNS). Methods Study Design and Setting:This prospective observational study was conducted between 2011 and 2020 at a university-affiliated tertiary pediatric nephrology center. The study aimed to evaluate the efficacy of rituximab in children with calcineurin inhibitor-resistant steroid-resistant nephrotic syndrome (SRNS) and to examine the association between renal histopathological findings and treatment response. Twenty-four children aged 2-12 years were enrolled.Follow-up:Patients were followed prospectively after completion of rituximab therapy through regular clinical and laboratory assessments. The mean follow-up duration after the last rituximab infusion was 5.1 years (range: 6 months-8 years).Treatment Response Definitions:Complete remission was defined according to International Pediatric Nephrology Association (IPNA) recommendations as a urine protein-to-creatinine ratio (UPCR) ≤20 mg/mmol (≤0.2 mg/mg) or negative/trace proteinuria on dipstick testing on at least three consecutive occasions.Partial remission was defined as a UPCR >20 mg/mmol but <200 mg/mmol together with serum albumin ≥30 g/L.No response was defined as failure to achieve either complete or partial remission.Genetic Evaluation:Genetic testing was performed in all patients with focal segmental glomerulosclerosis (FSGS), classic minimal change disease (MCD), and MCD with IgM deposition. No pathogenic or likely pathogenic variants associated with monogenic steroid-resistant nephrotic syndrome were identified in the tested patients. Genetic testing was not performed in patients with IgA nephropathy, membranous nephropathy, C1q nephropathy, or dense deposit disease. Results Twenty-four children with SRNS were included (13 males and 11 females; age range 2-12 years). Histopathological diagnoses included focal segmental glomerulosclerosis (FSGS) in 9 patients (37.5%), minimal change disease (MCD) in 4 (16.7%), MCD with IgM deposition in 6 (25.0%), dense deposit disease in 2 (8.3%), membranous nephropathy in 1 (4.2%), IgA nephropathy in 1 (4.2%), and C1q nephropathy in 1 (4.2%). Overall, 10 patients (41.7%) achieved complete remission and 3 (12.5%) achieved partial remission, predominantly among patients with MCD and MCD with IgM deposition. Responses were uncommon among patients with FSGS. Eleven patients (45.8%), all of whom were non-responders, progressed to end-stage kidney disease. No major adverse effects of rituximab were observed; mild infusion reactions occurred in three patients and mild cellulitis in one patient. Conclusion In this cohort of children with refractory SRNS, favorable responses to rituximab were observed predominantly among patients with CNI- resistant MCD and MCD with IgM deposition, whereas responses among patients with FSGS were uncommon. These findings suggest that renal histopathology may help identify patients more likely to benefit from rituximab therapy; however, the small sample size, heterogeneous histopathological distribution, and observational study design preclude definitive conclusions. Larger prospective multicenter studies incorporating comprehensive genetic evaluation are required to determine whether histopathology can serve as a reliable predictor of rituximab responsiveness.

title: Quantifying the Effect of Synthetic Colour Fundus Photograph Scaling on Foundation Models
abstract: Abstract Scaling synthetic colour fundus photographs (CFPs) offers a tunable strategy for retinal foundation-model pretraining. From 28,430 real CFPs, we generated 568,600 synthetic CFPs and compared six one-pass strategies: real-only, synthetic-only, real-plus-1×synthetic, real-plus-5×synthetic, real-plus-10×synthetic and real-plus-20×synthetic. Average area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) was highest in internal validation with real-plus-10×synthetic (0.906 versus 0.862 for real-only across 12 test datasets), but in external validation with real-plus-20×synthetic (0.777 versus 0.683 across eight datasets). The real-plus-1×synthetic strategy increased both averages with the lowest counted computation among real-plus-synthetic strategies. At a matched image count, synthetic-only achieved comparable average external AUROC to real-only. Generation accounted for approximately 99% of the estimated 9 × 10¹⁹ floating-point operations for generation and backbone pretraining. These findings identify complementary uses of synthetic scaling: lower-volume supplementation for a performance–computation balance and larger volumes for stronger external generalisation, with strategy selection guided by evaluation objectives and computational resources.

title: Predictive Value of Quantitative T2-Weighted MRI Morphometric Parameters for Clinically Significant Prostate Cancer in PI-RADS v2.1 ≥4 Lesions
abstract: Abstract Objective To evaluate the diagnostic accuracy of quantitative T2-weighted MRI morphometric parameters for detecting clinically significant prostate cancer (csPCa) in prostate lesions with PI-RADS v2.1 category ≥ 4. Methods This retrospective study included 153 patients who underwent multiparametric MRI according to the PI-RADS v2.1 protocol followed by prostate biopsy. A total of 165 prostate lesions with PI-RADS v2.1 scores ≥4were analyzed. Based on histopathological results, lesions were classified as csPCa or benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH). Quantitative morphometric parameters, including maximum diameter, mean diameter, cross-sectional area, and volume, were measured on tri-planar T2-weighted images. Differences between csPCa and BPH lesions, as well as zone-specific characteristics in the peripheral zone (PZ) and transition zone (TZ), were assessed. Receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve analysis was performed to evaluate the diagnostic performance of each parameter and to determine optimal cutoff values. Results Among the 165 lesions, 108 were csPCa (69 in the PZ and 39 in the TZ) and 57 were BPH (20 in the PZ and 37 in the TZ). csPCa lesions demonstrated significantly larger maximum diameter, mean diameter, area, and volume compared with BPH lesions in both the PZ and TZ (all p < 0.05). ROC analysis showed that lesion volume achieved the highest diagnostic performance among all morphometric parameters, with area under the curve (AUC) values of 0.819 in the PZ and 0.811 in the TZ. The optimal volume thresholds for differentiating csPCa from BPH were 1.23 cm³ in the PZ and 1.07 cm³ in the TZ, respectively. Conclusions In prostate lesions with PI-RADS v2.1 category ≥ 4, lesion volume demonstrates superior diagnostic accuracy compared with maximum diameter, mean diameter, and area. Volume-based assessment may serve as a valuable quantitative imaging biomarker to improve the detection of clinically significant prostate cancer, particularly when accounting for zone-specific differences.

Conclusions In prostate lesions with PI-RADS v2.1 category ≥ 4, lesion volume demonstrates superior diagnostic accuracy compared with maximum diameter, mean diameter, and area. title: Clinical criteria for suspected early hip osteoarthritis at the earliest radiographic stage: an international Technical Expert Panel study
abstract: Abstract Background Early hip osteoarthritis (EHOA) remains challenging to recognise at presentation, particularly when symptoms are recent and radiographic abnormalities are absent or minimal. Standardised clinical criteria for this stage are limited. This study aimed to develop expert-derived criteria for identifying suspected EHOA at the earliest radiographic stage and to propose monitoring suggestions. Methods An international, multidisciplinary Technical Expert Panel study was conducted, supported by a structured literature review and expert panel voting. Candidate items were generated from the literature review and face-to-face expert discussion, then organised into domains and subdomains. Items were included in the final framework when they achieved > 66% agreement. The perceived strength of each retained item was rated on a 0–10 numerical scale. Results The final framework included two overarching areas: criteria for identifying suspected EHOA and suggestions for careful monitoring. Five domains were retained for identification: exclusion/applicability criteria, symptoms and signs, risk factors, time framework and imaging. Key clinical indicators included load-related mechanical pain, pain during hip rotation, brief start-up or morning stiffness, walking limitation and difficulty with squatting, getting in or out of a car, and putting on socks. Supportive risk factors included elevated body mass index, previous hip symptoms, occupational loading, high-level sports participation, previous hip injury or surgery, family history, femoroacetabular impingement, hip dysplasia, Legg-Calve-Perthes disease, slipped capital femoral epiphysis and leg-length discrepancy. A symptom duration of < 6 months was retained as the preferred timeframe. Baseline radiography was emphasised to exclude established OA, while MRI and ultrasound were considered selective complementary tools. Conclusions This Technical Expert Panel proposes a clinical framework for identifying suspected EHOA at the earliest radiographic stage and guiding careful monitoring. Prospective studies are required to validate its diagnostic and prognostic performance before clinical implementation as formal criteria.

title: Lightweight Pure 3D Lung Nodule Detection and Segmentation Network with Asymmetric Feature Interaction
abstract: Abstract Three-dimensional convolutional neural networks (3D CNNs) for lung nodule analysis face a tension between accuracy and computational cost: isotropic cubic kernels match anisotropic CT data poorly, detection and segmentation are modeled in isolation, and parameter-constrained networks collapse to the trivial all-background solution under class imbalance. This study proposes Light3D-NoduleNet, a lightweight pure 3D joint detection and segmentation network for edge deployment. An asymmetric 3D depthwise separable convolution factorizes the cubic kernel into in-plane and inter-slice branches, cutting kernel parameters by about 56%; a scale-aware efficient channel attention adapts its kernel size to the channel count; and a bidirectional feature interaction module exchanges a spatial attention map and a channel attention vector between the two branches, closing the loop between tasks. Joint training on LUNA16 and LIDC-IDRI uses dynamic loss masking. On LIDC-IDRI, the model reaches a Dice coefficient of 0.5233 (median 95% Hausdorff distance 6.00 mm) with 5.24 M parameters and 178.3 G FLOPs, exceeding reproduced 3D U-Net and V-Net by 0.1545 and 0.0701. Three variants lacking bidirectional interaction all stagnate at 0.2302 after 100 epochs, whereas the full model converges to 0.5233. On a 15 W Jetson Orin NX it runs at 3.0 FPS with 435 MB VRAM, indicating that bidirectional feature interaction is a necessary architectural condition for lightweight 3D networks to escape the trivial solution under extreme foreground-background imbalance.

title: Ultrasound Deep Learning for Distinguishing Benign Reactive from Hematologic Malignancy-Associated Cervical Lymphadenopathy in Children: Development and Validation
abstract: Abstract Background Cervical lymphadenopathy is a common reason for pediatric outpatient visits. It is usually reactive but may also accompany leukemia or lymphoma. Because these conditions may have overlapping ultrasound appearances, we developed a deep-learning model to distinguish benign reactive from hematologic malignancy-associated cervical lymphadenopathy. The model may provide valuable support for diagnosing hematologic malignancies and guiding differential diagnosis in pediatric outpatient practice. Methods This single-center retrospective study included 653 cervical lymph-node annotations after four duplicate images with discordant diagnoses were excluded. The benign reactive group comprised 283 annotations, and the hematologic malignancy-associated group comprised 370. Related images were kept in the same data fold, yielding 559 non-redundant image groups for analysis. An ImageNet-pretrained EfficientNetV2-S model using consensus lesion masks was evaluated with grouped nested five-fold cross-validation. Model probabilities were calibrated with Platt scaling. The primary endpoint was the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC); accuracy, sensitivity, specificity, predictive values, and the Brier score were also assessed. Results The model achieved an AUC of 0.863 (95% confidence interval, 0.834 to 0.893) and an average precision of 0.865. At the Youden operating point, accuracy was 0.784, sensitivity was 0.773, specificity was 0.796, and positive predictive value was 0.824. The calibrated Brier score was 0.154. AUCs for the four diagnosis-specific comparisons ranged from 0.839 to 0.883. Conclusions Ultrasound image analysis showed good internal discrimination between benign reactive and hematologic malignancy-associated cervical lymphadenopathy in children. These findings support multicenter, patient-level evaluation of the model as an adjunct to ultrasound assessment.This model could provide radiologists and other clinicians with decision support for the non-invasive ultrasound assessment of cervical lymphadenopathy in children.

title: MVMGNN: Multi-View Masked Graph Neural Network for Alzheimer’s Disease Diagnosis using Structural MRI
abstract: Abstract Alzheimer’s disease (AD) is a prevalent neurodegenerative disorder, and early diagnosis is essential for timely intervention. Structural magnetic resonance imaging (sMRI) provides valuable information for characterizing AD-related brain alterations. However, existing sMRI-based brain graph methods often rely on single graph construction strategies, limiting their ability to capture complementary spatial and morphological relationships among brain regions. Moreover, multi-view approaches may introduce redundant features and noisy connections without effective selection and fusion mechanisms.To address these issues, we propose a Multi-View Masked Graph Neural Network (MVMGNN) for AD diagnosis using sMRI data. Brain regions are represented as graph nodes with radiomics features, and two complementary graph views are constructed based on spatial proximity and feature similarity. A joint node–edge masking mechanism is introduced to adaptively select informative feature dimensions and structural connections. In addition, a patient-level cross-view gated fusion module is developed to integrate multi-view representations. Experimental results on the ADNI dataset demonstrate that MVMGNN achieves competitive performance compared with existing methods across AD-related classification tasks. Interpretability analysis further reveals discriminative brain regions and structural connections associated with AD, providing insights into sMRI-based brain network analysis.

title: Vision Foundation Models for Multi-Modal Medical Image Classification
abstract: Abstract Clinicians combine several imaging modalities to reach a diagnosis. Yet assembling large annotated datasets for every modality combination is rarely feasible, and modalities are frequently missing in practice. Vision foundation models (FMs) could ease both problems by transferring from few labels, but this has mainly been shown for single images. We therefore compare FM initialisation (DINOv2 and MedSigLIP) against random initialisation, across fusion and training strategies, on three tasks: glioma subtyping from multi-sequence MRI, HER2 scoring from paired histopathology stains, and liver-lesion classification from multi-phase MRI. At full data, FM initialisation matched or outperformed random initialisation, raising liver-lesion sensitivity from 54 % to 76 %. The advantage held as labels grew scarce and was largest under missing modalities, where FM initialisation kept sensitivity near 73 % as random initialisation fell to 29 %. For multi-modal medical imaging, FM initialisation is a strong default, most valuable when labels are scarce or acquisition protocols incomplete.

title: Analyzing the Prognostic Value of Radiomic Variables from PET-CT with [18F]FDG in a Retrospective Cohort of Patients with Adrenocortical Carcinoma
abstract: Abstract Objective To evaluate whether radiomic features extracted from [ 18 F]FDG PET/CT are associated with established prognostic factors and survival outcomes in patients with adrenocortical carcinoma (ACC) in an exploratory proof-of-concept study. Methods In this retrospective study, 22 patients with histologically confirmed ACC who underwent pretreatment [ 18 F]FDG PET/CT were included. Conventional PET metrics (SUVmax, SUVmean, MTV, and TLG) and radiomic features were extracted. Dimensionality reduction was performed using principal component analysis (PCA). Machine learning models were developed to predict 5-year survival. Interobserver reproducibility was assessed using the Dice similarity coefficient (DSC). Associations between imaging parameters and clinical-pathological variables were evaluated statistically. Results Interobserver agreement for tumor segmentation was high (mean DSC = 86.2% ± 6.0%). The Naive Bayes model based on both PET and CT data achieved the highest accuracy among all other models (AUC = 0.750). Conventional PET parameters were not significantly correlated with Ki-67 or Weiss score; however, higher TLG had a non-significant association with p53-positive tumors in this small sample (p = 0.065). Conclusions Radiomic features derived from [ 18 F]FDG PET/CT demonstrate potential prognostic value in ACC. PET-based models outperformed CT-based models. Larger multicenter studies are warranted to validate these findings.

title: Diagnostic Value of Peripheral Zone PSA Density for Detecting Clinically Significant Prostate Cancer in Men with Peripheral Zone MRI Lesions Running title: Peripheral Zone PSA Density in Prostate Cancer
abstract: Abstract Background Whole-gland prostate-specific antigen density (PSAD) may underestimate the diagnostic contribution of peripheral zone (PZ) tumors, as it is diluted by transition zone (TZ) volume, which expands with age independent of cancer risk. We investigated whether PZ-specific PSAD (PSAD_PZ) improves the detection of clinically significant prostate cancer (csPCa) in men with PZ-only multiparametric MRI (mpMRI) target lesions, and evaluated the analogous TZ-specific PSAD (PSAD_TZ) in men with TZ-only targets. Methods We analyzed 651 men from the prospectively enrolled SUPER-PC registry, supplemented by a retrospectively identified non-cancer cohort, who underwent combined systematic and MRI-targeted fusion biopsy (416 with PZ-only and 235 with TZ-only mpMRI targets). Clinically significant prostate cancer was defined as International Society of Urological Pathology Grade Group 2 or greater. The diagnostic performance of PSA, whole-gland PSAD, and zone-specific PSAD was compared using receiver operating characteristic curve analysis, and optimal cut-off values were determined using the Youden index. Results In the PZ-target group, PSAD_PZ achieved a significantly higher area under the curve (AUC) than PSA (0.825 vs. 0.707, p < 0.001) and whole-gland PSAD (0.825 vs. 0.702, p < 0.001). This advantage persisted among men with Prostate Imaging Reporting and Data System (PI-RADS) category 4 or higher lesions (AUC 0.842) and remained significant after multivariable adjustment. The optimal PSAD_PZ cut-off value was 0.285 ng/mL/cm³, yielding a sensitivity of 70.8% and specificity of 84.3%. PSAD_TZ did not outperform PSA or whole-gland PSAD in the TZ-target group. Conclusions PSAD_PZ improves the detection of csPCa in men with PZ-only mpMRI targets and outperforms conventional whole-gland PSAD, supporting a zone-matched normalization strategy that may help reduce unnecessary biopsies and guide treatment decisions. PSAD_TZ conferred no comparable benefit among men with TZ-only targets.

title: CT Colonography as a Triage Examination After a Positive Fecal Immunochemical Test: A Retrospective Cohort Study in a Chilean Screening Program
abstract: Abstract Purpose: To evaluate computed tomography colonography (CTC) as a triage examination for colonoscopy within a fecal immunochemical test (FIT)-based colorectal cancer screening program in a resource-limited region of Chile. Methods: This retrospective cohort study included asymptomatic FIT-positive individuals aged 45–75 years who underwent CTC between January 2019 and November 2022. Patients with CT Colonography Reporting and Data System (C-RADS) C2–C4 findings were referred for optical colonoscopy. The primary outcome was the per-patient positive predictive value (PPV) of CTC for polyps measuring ≥ 6 mm among patients with an evaluable colonoscopy. Results: The cohort comprised 675 patients (mean age 64.0 years, SD 9.2; 443 women, 65.6%). Overall, 473 patients (70.1%) were classified as C1 and were not referred for immediate colonoscopy, 62 (9.2%) had C3–C4 findings and 71 (10.5%) had unresolved C0 examinations. Of 131 patients referred for colonoscopy, 115 (87.8%) underwent the procedure and 108 had an evaluable examination. Colonoscopy confirmed at least one polyp measuring ≥ 6 mm in 93 patients, yielding a PPV of 86.1% (95% CI 78.3–91.4). Advanced colorectal neoplasia was confirmed in 48 patients (PPV 44.4%, 95% CI 35.4–53.8). The detection rates was 42/675 (6.2%) for advanced adenoma and 6/675 (0.9%) for colorectal cancer. Conclusion: Among FIT-positive patients with CTC findings warranting colonoscopy, clinically relevant colorectal lesions were frequently confirmed. CTC may help prioritize colonoscopy in settings with limited endoscopic capacity. Further evaluation of the complete screening pathway is warranted.

title: Ethmoidal alveolar rhabdomyosarcoma with orbital extension in a young adult: A case report and literature review
abstract: Abstract Background Rhabdomyosarcoma (RMS) is an uncommon malignant neoplasm of skeletal muscle differentiation that predominantly affects children. Sinonasal RMS is rare in adults, and the alveolar subtype tends toward aggressive local growth with regional and distant spread. Its clinical and radiologic presentation can overlap with inflammatory, infectious, and other malignant sinonasal processes, which makes diagnosis difficult. Case presentation A 28-year-old Middle Eastern man presented with a one-week history of right-sided proptosis and right eye pain, associated with diplopia and painful upward gaze but without prominent sinonasal symptoms. Computed tomography demonstrated a heterogeneous expansile mass centered in the right ethmoid and maxillary sinuses with extension through the lamina papyracea into the right orbit. Endoscopic sinus surgery with tumor debulking and biopsy demonstrated erosion of the lamina papyracea and extensive involvement of the ethmoid air cells. Histopathology showed an infiltrative malignant small round blue cell neoplasm arranged in nests and lobules separated by delicate fibrovascular stroma, with brisk mitotic activity, including seven mitotic figures per high-power field. Tumor cells showed diffuse strong nuclear expression of myogenin and MyoD1 and retained INI1. Pan-cytokeratin, CK5/6, chromogranin, synaptophysin, S100, CD99, FLI1, CD20, and CD3 were negative. Molecular testing was positive for FOXO1 rearrangement, supporting the diagnosis of alveolar rhabdomyosarcoma. Staging demonstrated no definite distant metastatic disease. Systemic chemotherapy with ifosfamide and etoposide was initiated, and the patient remains under treatment and follow-up. Conclusion Adult sinonasal alveolar rhabdomyosarcoma is rare and can be difficult to diagnose; it may present with orbital manifestations despite limited sinonasal symptoms. Its characteristic morphology, myogenic immunophenotype, and FOXO1 rearrangement help establish the diagnosis. Management requires a multidisciplinary team and careful evaluation of orbital and intracranial extension.

title: Sonographic Appearance of Congenital Cervical Teratoma: A Case Report
abstract: Abstract Background : Cervical teratomas account for only 3–9% of neonatal teratomas. Although usually benign, they may cause significant airway compression, necessitating prompt diagnosis and surgical intervention. Cervical teratomas are typically cystic or cystic-solid and often contain calcifications; a predominantly solid, hypervascular mass without calcification is rare and may pose a diagnostic challenge. We report such a case to highlight its atypical sonographic features and the diagnostic value of combining ultrasound with color Doppler imaging and ultrasound-guided fine-needle aspiration (FNA). Case presentation : A six-hour-old female neonate was transferred for respiratory distress after tracheal intubation. Physical examination revealed a firm midline cervical mass (4×3×5cm). Ultrasonography showed a predominantly solid, heterogeneously echogenic mass with irregular margins and increased vascularity. Contrast-enhanced computed tomography (CT) demonstrated mild enhancement with tracheal displacement, and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) confirmed tracheal compression. Ultrasound-guided FNA yielded fibrous and cartilaginous elements, supporting the diagnosis of teratoma. The tumor was surgically resected, and histopathology confirmed a mature solid teratoma. Conclusions : Cervical teratomas may present atypically as predominantly solid, hypervascular masses without detectable calcification. In neonates with respiratory distress and a cervical mass, prompt diagnosis and surgery are imperative. Ultrasonography combined with color Doppler imaging and FNA provides valuable preoperative information for surgical decision-making.

Ultrasound-guided FNA yielded fibrous and cartilaginous elements, supporting the diagnosis of teratoma. The tumor was surgically resected, and histopathology confirmed a mature solid teratoma. Conclusions : Cervical teratomas may present atypically as predominantly solid, hypervascular masses without detectable calcification. In neonates with respiratory distress and a cervical mass, prompt diagnosis and surgery are imperative. Ultrasonography combined with color Doppler imaging and FNA provides valuable preoperative information for surgical decision-making.

title: Sex differences in quantitative fundus parameters measured by artificial intelligence: a cross-sectional community study
abstract: Abstract Background Automated analysis of fundus photographs yields numerous quantitative measures, but sex differences in these measures and their modification by systemic conditions are not well characterized. We quantified these differences in a large community screening cohort. Methods This cross-sectional study included 21,844 participants contributing 32,576 eye-level records to a community health-screening program in Ganzhou, China. EVisionAI was used to quantify 49 vascular, optic disc and cup, peripapillary atrophy, and fundus tessellation density parameters from color fundus photographs. Generalized estimating equations clustered by participant estimated male-female differences in standardized parameters. Models were unadjusted, adjusted for age and age squared, and further adjusted for 20 binary systemic conditions. Sex-by-condition interactions were examined for 19 conditions; prostatic hyperplasia was assessed separately using a three-level variable. Benjamini–Hochberg correction was applied across all fundus parameters within each model for the primary comparisons and within each condition for the interaction analyses. Results Mean age was 63.6 ± 9.8 years in women and 63.9 ± 10.1 years in men. After full adjustment and FDR correction, sex differences were found in 41 of 49 parameters: 19 of 22 optic disc and cup, 8 of 11 vascular, 7 of 7 peripapillary atrophy, and 7 of 9 fundus tessellation density measures. The largest standardized differences in men were a lower disc vertical-to-horizontal ratio (β = −0.170; 95% confidence interval, − 0.196 to − 0.144) and a higher atrophy arc height-to-disc vertical diameter ratio (β = 0.166; 95% confidence interval, 0.141 to 0.192). The arteriole-to-venule ratio was also lower in men (β = −0.113; 95% confidence interval, − 0.137 to − 0.089). Estimates were generally stable across models. Twenty-three effect-modification findings remained significant after false discovery rate correction, predominantly involving prostatic hyperplasia. Conclusions Sex differences were present across most quantitative fundus parameters and changed little after adjustment for measured systemic conditions. Their relevance to screening requires validation in datasets with ocular biometry and clinical outcomes.

title: Habitat Radiomics-Based Stacking Ensemble Model for Predicting Disease-Free Survival in Early-Stage Cervical Cancer
abstract: Abstract Purpose Despite undergoing curative surgery, about 30% of patients with early-stage cervical cancer (ECC) face the risk of recurrence. However, current prognostic tools are not very effective, with concordance index (C-index) typically ranging from 0.60 to 0.70. This study aimed to develop and validate a stacking survival ensemble model that incorporates intratumoral and peritumoral habitat radiomic features derived from routine preoperative multiparametric MRI to predict postoperative disease-free survival (DFS) in ECC. Methods This retrospective-prospective study enrolled 583 ECC patients (training: n = 293, internal validation: n = 165, external validation: n = 125). Habitat radiomic features were extracted from intratumoral and 3-mm peritumoral regions on preoperative T2WI, DWI, and CE-T1WI. A two-tier stacking survival ensemble framework was constructed with five base survival models (Cox regression, Random Survival Forest, Elastic Net-Cox, DeepSurv, and Support Vector Regression) and a Cox regression Meta-learner. Performance was assessed by C-index, time-dependent AUC, calibration curves, and decision curve analysis. The incremental value of the model-derived lymph node metastasis probability (pLNM) from our prior classification model was also evaluated. Results The Meta-model achieved C-indices of 0.878, 0.868, and 0.848 in the training, internal validation, and external validation cohorts, outperforming most base models (P < 0.05). Externally, it yielded time-dependent AUCs of 0.887, 0.875, and 0.860 at 12, 24, and 36 months. Kaplan-Meier analysis showed that the Meta-model effectively stratified into high- and low-risk groups with distinct DFS outcomes (log-rank P < 0.001 for all cohorts). Adding pLNM further improved C-index from 0.878 to 0.913 in the training cohort (P < 0.001). Conclusion The stacking survival ensemble model enables accurate postoperative risk stratification for ECC patients using routine preoperative MRI without additional imaging, potentially guiding individualized adjuvant therapy and surveillance intensity.

title: Exploring the Spectrum of Clinical and Radiological Findings in Active Tuberculosis
abstract: Abstract Background Clinical data may not accurately diagnose pulmonary tuberculosis (PTB), mainly due to manifestation overlap with other diseases, causing delays and misdiagnoses. Many gaps in the interpretation of clinical and radiographic findings were addressed and updated in our study. Methods An institutional-based study was carried out between 02/01/2018 and 26/06/2020 to clinically assess TB outpatients in high-burden zones. Those patients were identified through smear microscopy, GeneXpert Ultra, and chest X-rays and TB positives were interviewed. Of total, 329 patients were enrolled from Bench-Skeko, 23 from Skeka, and 29 from Keffa. Both descriptive and inferential statistics were performed using Stata 14/16. Results A total of 410 TB confirmed cases, with 328 (80%) being PTB, 79 (19.3%) EPTB, and 3 (0.73%) involving both forms were involved in this study. The mean age was 27.65 ± 11.44 years, with 55% male. Most patients were recently identified (99.3%). GeneXpert was used in 62.4%, AFB in 8.78%, and lesion biopsy or FNAC for EPTB in 16.83%, and 98% was on the intensive therapy for susceptible TB. A febrile episode was diagnosed in 93% (5.4% >40°C, 87% <39°C), night sweat in 93.17%, appetite loss in 89%, fatigue in 90%, and weight loss in 88%. Respiratory symptoms were very common, with cough reported in 94.2%: productive in 91%, and prolonged (> 3 wks) in 77%. Abnormalities in chest X ray were reported in 16.3%, with pleural effusion in 11.2%, cavitary formations in 13%, and lymph node enlarged in 14%. Blood pressure abnormalities were relatively low, with 76.3% having normal. Only few findings were reported as statistically significant predictors of active PTB. Chest abnormalities (OR = 6.87), prolonged cough (OR = 6.4), mucoid (OR = 14.6), and mucopurulent sputum (OR = 56.4) increased PTB odds, while lymphadenopathy was less commonly reported (OR = 0.16). Appetite loss (OR = 3.26), pleural effusion (OR = 2.41), and fibrosis (OR = 2.31) showed weak associations. Conclusions A high prevalence of the TB tetrad: prolonged cough, night sweat, fever and appetite loss were observed. PTB odds were higher with chest abnormalities, effusion, fibrosis, infiltration, and expansion, highlighting the diagnostic value of radiology. Clinical Trial Registration : No applicable

title: Unsupervised multimodal brain MRI registration with complementary learned and structural descriptors.
abstract: Abstract Deformable registration of T1- and T2-weighted brain magnetic resonance images is difficult because tissue intensities differ across contrasts. We investigate whether learned and hand-crafted descriptors provide complementary similarity information for unsupervised registration. A Cross-Modal Descriptor Network learns contrast-invariant voxel embeddings through self-supervised contrastive training on aligned same-subject pairs. These embeddings are combined with the modality-independent neighbourhood descriptor with self-similarity context (MIND-SSC) to train a compact diffeomorphic attention U-Net without anatomical labels. In inter-subject T1-to-T2 registration on the IXI dataset (n=45), the hybrid achieved a mean Dice coefficient of 0.700 and a 95th-percentile Hausdorff distance of 3.21 mm, with no observed folded voxels. It outperformed the evaluated classical, learned, structural-descriptor, transformer, and foundation-model baselines (p<0.05, paired Wilcoxon tests). Gains were largest for small deep gray-matter structures, and the hybrid also performed best in the evaluated unseen-scanner and BraTS glioma experiments. Descriptors are used only during training; inference requires one 83 ms forward pass of a 0.247 M-parameter network. These results support combining learned and structural descriptors for accurate and computationally efficient multimodal brain registration.
